label: L13
title: R.O.A.D. I to Precision Medicine
brief: Lecture 13 presents the R.O.A.D. framework for finding heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE) in observational data and for full use of RCT data, instead of one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analysis. A baseline-risk model is trained on untreated patients and applied to everyone, patients are split into risk buckets, and a per-bucket assignment MIO matches each treated patient to a distinct untreated patient to emulate an RCT. Matching does not remove unobserved confounding, so the treated-arm counterfactual model up-weights treated patients without recurrence by $\rho$. An Optimal Policy Tree then assigns treatment to minimize predicted recurrence, and recommendations are validated (and $\rho$ tuned) with sensitivity and specificity. Applications: adjuvant imatinib for GIST (MSK training, Polish external validation, compared with PERSIST-5) and radiotherapy for extremity sarcoma (trained on an MSK RCT). Expect questions on the matching formulation and its constraints, why and in which direction $\rho$ corrects confounding, the OPT objective, and reading the sensitivity/specificity results.
kp: RCTs are the gold standard but expensive, slow, tuned to the average patient; one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analysis is a clear limitation.
Data $(x_i,t_i,y_i)$; GIST: $t_i=1$ if imatinib, $y_i=1$ if recurrence.
Confounding: higher-risk patients got imatinib, so treated mean outcomes were worse although imatinib does not raise recurrence risk.
Baseline risk $w_i=g_\theta(x_i)$, with $g_\theta$ trained on $t_i=0$ only, applied to all; split into $m$ risk buckets $b_i$.

Per-bucket matching MIO: $\min_z\sum_{i\in S_1^k}\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|$ s.t. $\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}=1\ \forall i\in S_1^k$, $\sum_{i\in S_1^k}z_{ij}\le1\ \forall j\in S_0^k$, $z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$; gives $n_1^k=n_0^k$.
Matching reduces prognostic heterogeneity on observed covariates only; unobserved confounders remain in the $t_i=1$ group.

Counterfactual models: $h_{t=0}$ with plain empirical loss on $S_0$; $h_{t=1}$ with loss $\frac{1}{n_1^s}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_1^-}\ell(y_i,h_{t=1}(x_i))+\rho\sum_{j\in S_1^+}\ell(y_j,h_{t=1}(x_j))\Big)$.
Sensitivity = recurred & recommended / all recurred; specificity = not recurred & not recommended / all not recurred. Higher $\rho$: sensitivity up, specificity down.
GIST: $\rho\ge2$ needed (7-yr RFS 83% vs 82%); Polish validation sens 89%, spec 70% vs PERSIST-5 91%/63%. Sarcoma RT: sens 90%, spec 15%, age cutoff 52 vs RCT's 60.

topics.x: RCTs are expensive, long, and answer questions for the average patient; their subgroup analyses split on one baseline variable at a time. Observational data are cheap and plentiful but confounded. R.O.A.D. aims to extract HTE from observational data and to use RCT data beyond the ATE.

Each GIST patient is $(x_i,t_i,y_i)$ with $t_i=1$ for imatinib and $y_i=1$ for recurrence. Physicians gave imatinib to higher-risk patients, so treated outcomes look worse, a signature of confounding bias.

Train $g_\theta$ on untreated patients, score everyone, and bucket by baseline risk. In each bucket solve an assignment MIO that matches every treated patient to a distinct untreated patient minimizing covariate distance, so the matched cohort emulates an RCT. Unobserved confounding remains.

Fit $h_{t=0}$ on matched untreated and $h_{t=1}$ on matched treated patients. The treated loss multiplies the loss of treated non-recurrences by $\rho$, pushing $h_{t=1}$ toward lower risk to offset the worse unobserved prognosis of treated patients.

An OPT picks $\tau(x)\in\{0,1\}$ per leaf to minimize the sum of predicted recurrence risks. Recommendations are scored by sensitivity (recurred patients who were recommended treatment) and specificity (non-recurred patients spared treatment); these metrics also tune $\rho$ and check robustness across OPTs.

536 MSK patients, random-forest baseline model, survival RF counterfactual models. $\rho\ge2$ was needed before predicted 7-year RFS under imatinib exceeded no imatinib. External validation on 557 Polish patients: sensitivity 89%, specificity 70%, higher specificity than PERSIST-5; OPT found 3 subgroups without and 2 with benefit.

Training on a 164-patient MSK RCT of adjuvant radiotherapy (brachytherapy) with oversampling of higher-risk strata. Validation on 936 untreated MSK patients: sensitivity 90%, specificity 15%, age cutoff 52 vs the RCT's univariate 60. Claimed benefits: cheaper and faster than RCTs, fairer, and full use of RCT data.

cards.b: Variation in how the treatment effect differs across patients.
cards.x: RCTs answer for the average patient; HTE is what precision medicine needs and RCTs do not deliver.

cards.f: Main limitation of classic RCT subgroup analysis
cards.b: It is one-variable-at-a-time: patients are split sequentially on single baseline characteristics.
cards.x: RCTs also do not define subgroups from combinations of patient characteristics; OPTs split on several variables jointly.

cards.b: $(x_i,t_i,y_i)$: covariates (mitotic count, tumor site, size), $t_i=1$ if imatinib, $y_i=1$ if recurrence.
cards.x: Outcome is binary recurrence, so lower predicted $y$ is better.

cards.f: Evidence of confounding in the GIST data
cards.b: Imatinib-treated patients had worse mean outcomes than untreated ones, although imatinib does not increase recurrence risk.
cards.x: Physicians offered imatinib to patients with worse baseline risk, so naive comparison penalizes the drug.

cards.b: ML model trained on untreated patients ($t_i=0$) to predict recurrence; $w_i=g_\theta(x_i)$ is then computed for all patients.
cards.x: Training only on untreated patients gives a risk under no treatment that is comparable across arms.

cards.b: Split patients into $m$ buckets, each an interval of baseline risk estimates $w_i$; patient becomes $(x_i,t_i,y_i,w_i,b_i)$.
cards.x: Matching inside buckets ensures treated and untreated are compared at the same baseline risk.

cards.b: $\min_z\sum_{i\in S_1^k}\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|$ s.t. $\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}=1\ \forall i\in S_1^k$, $\sum_{i\in S_1^k}z_{ij}\le1\ \forall j\in S_0^k$, $z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$
cards.x: An assignment problem: every treated patient gets exactly one untreated match, every untreated patient is used at most once.

cards.b: Make $n_1^k=n_0^k$ in each bucket $k$, so within a bucket a patient is equally likely to be treated or not, as in an RCT.
cards.x: Equal counts per risk stratum is what makes the cohort emulate a randomized trial.

cards.b: Unobserved confounding: the $t_i=1$ group still has worse outcomes than its baseline estimates, so outcome differences cannot be attributed to treatment.
cards.x: The baseline model was trained on $t_i=0$, so it cannot see unobserved factors that drove treatment.

cards.f: Loss for the treated counterfactual model $h_{t=1}$
cards.x: $S_1^+$ are treated patients without recurrence; $S_1^-$ treated with recurrence. $h_{t=0}$ uses the unweighted average loss on $S_0$.

cards.b: The model fits treated non-recurrences better, so $h_{t=1}$ predicts lower recurrence risk under treatment.
cards.x: This offsets unobserved worse prognosis of treated patients; too large a $\rho$ over-recommends treatment.
Each patient is charged the predicted recurrence risk of the arm the tree assigns, so the tree minimizes predicted recurrences.

cards.b: Recurred patients for whom OPT recommended treatment, divided by all recurred patients (recommended + not recommended).
cards.x: Computed on untreated patients, assuming the drug would have prevented the recurrences.

cards.b: Non-recurred patients for whom OPT did not recommend treatment, divided by all non-recurred patients.
cards.x: 80% specificity: of 100 untreated non-recurrers, 80 are spared unnecessary treatment.

cards.b: $\rho\ge2$: at 2, predicted 7-yr RFS under imatinib (83%) exceeded no imatinib (82%); at 1.5 it was still lower (79% vs 82%).
cards.x: Tried $\rho\in[1.5,3.25]$; below 2 residual unobserved confounding still made the drug look harmful.

cards.b: 557 Polish patients: OPT sensitivity 89%, specificity 70%, vs PERSIST-5 RCT 91% and 63%.
cards.x: Similar sensitivity, higher specificity: fewer patients treated unnecessarily.

cards.b: 936 MSK patients without RT: sensitivity 90%, specificity 15%; various OPTs 88-90% and 15-21%.
cards.x: RT is given to all limb-sparing surgery patients today, so sparing 15% who would not benefit is meaningful.

quiz.q: What does heterogeneity of treatment effects (HTE) refer to?
o: Variation in treatment effect across patients
Variation in treatment dose across hospitals
Differences in outcome definitions across trials
Random noise in the observed outcomes
quiz.e: HTE is how the effect of a treatment differs between patients, which RCTs aimed at the average patient do not capture. Noise in outcomes is not an effect difference.

quiz.q: In the GIST setup, what does $y_i=1$ mean?
o: Patient $i$ had a recurrence
Patient $i$ received imatinib
Patient $i$ is in risk bucket 1
Patient $i$ was matched to a control
quiz.e: $y_i$ is the outcome (recurrence); the treatment indicator is $t_i$.

quiz.q: On which patients is the baseline risk model $g_\theta$ trained?
o: Untreated patients only ($t_i=0$)
Treated patients only ($t_i=1$)
All patients, with $t_i$ as a feature
Matched pairs from every bucket
quiz.e: $g_\theta$ is trained on $t_i=0$ and then applied to the treated group to estimate baseline (no-treatment) risk. Using $t_i$ as a feature would mix treatment into the baseline score.

quiz.q: OPT sensitivity is defined as:
o: Recurred & recommended treatment / all recurred
Recommended treatment & recurred / all recommended
Not recurred & not recommended / all not recurred
Recurred & not recommended / all recommended
quiz.e: Sensitivity is among patients who recurred (and would have benefited). The third option is specificity; the second is a precision-type ratio.

quiz.q: In the RCT application, which treatment did the OPT evaluate?
o: Adjuvant radiotherapy for extremity or truncal sarcoma
Adjuvant imatinib for gastrointestinal stromal tumors
Postoperative chemotherapy for liposarcoma
Limb-sparing surgery versus amputation
quiz.e: The RCT case is adjuvant RT (brachytherapy) after limb-sparing surgery. Imatinib for GIST is the observational case.

quiz.q: Which is listed as a benefit of the R.O.A.D. approach in the conclusions?
o: Fairness by including groups underrepresented in RCTs
Removing the need for any external validation
Guaranteeing unbiased average treatment effects
Replacing outcome models with propensity scores
quiz.e: The slides list fairness via women and minorities historically underrepresented in RCTs. The method itself relies on external validation.

quiz.q: In the MSK GIST data, imatinib-treated patients had worse mean outcomes. The slides conclude:
o: Confounding: higher-risk patients were more likely to get imatinib
Imatinib increases the risk of recurrence
The recurrence outcome was mislabeled in the treated group
The sample was too small to compare the two groups
quiz.e: Treatment was not randomized and physicians gave imatinib to worse-prognosis patients. Since imatinib does not raise recurrence risk, worse treated outcomes signal confounding.

quiz.q: In the per-bucket matching MIO, what does $\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}=1\ \forall i\in S_1^k$ enforce?
o: Every treated patient is matched to exactly one untreated patient
Every untreated patient is matched to exactly one treated patient
Each bucket contains exactly one treated patient
Total matching distance in a bucket equals one
quiz.e: The sum runs over controls $j$ for a fixed treated $i$. The reverse direction is constrained by $\sum_i z_{ij}\le1$, which only caps reuse of controls.

quiz.q: What does the constraint $\sum_{i\in S_1^k}z_{ij}\le1\ \forall j\in S_0^k$ ensure?
o: No untreated patient is used as a match more than once
Every untreated patient must be matched
Each treated patient has at most one match
Matched pairs are within distance 1 of each other
quiz.e: It caps each control's usage at one, so matching is without replacement. It is an inequality, so some untreated patients may stay unmatched.

quiz.q: Why is the matching problem solved separately within each risk bucket?
o: To get equal treated and untreated counts at each baseline risk level
Because the full problem would be infeasible with binary variables
To let each bucket use a different distance metric
To make the baseline risk model consistent across buckets
quiz.e: Requiring $n_1^k=n_0^k$ per bucket balances treatment across risk strata, emulating randomization. Solving per bucket also keeps the problem small, but balance is the stated goal.

quiz.q: In the loss for $h_{t=1}$, which patients are weighted by $\rho$?
o: Treated patients who did not have a recurrence ($S_1^+$)
Treated patients who had a recurrence ($S_1^-$)
Untreated patients who did not have a recurrence
All matched patients in the highest risk bucket
quiz.e: $\rho$ multiplies the loss over $S_1^+$. Up-weighting $S_1^-$ would push $h_{t=1}$ toward higher risk, worsening the confounding bias.

quiz.q: What does the OPT objective minimize?
o: Sum over patients of predicted recurrence risk under the assigned arm
Number of patients assigned to treatment
Misclassification of the observed treatment $t_i$
Squared error between $h_{t=1}$ and $h_{t=0}$
quiz.e: Each patient contributes $h_{t=0}(x_i)$ or $h_{t=1}(x_i,\rho)$ depending on $\tau(x_i)$, so the tree minimizes predicted recurrences. It does not imitate historical treatment.

quiz.q: An OPT has 80% specificity. This means:
o: Of 100 untreated non-recurrers, 80 were not recommended treatment
Of 100 untreated recurrers, 80 were recommended treatment
80% of recommended patients would recur without treatment
80% of patients follow the OPT recommendation
quiz.e: Specificity counts non-recurrers correctly spared treatment. The second option describes sensitivity.

quiz.q: In the GIST tuning table, as $\rho$ rises from 1.5 to 3.25, OPT sensitivity and specificity:
o: Sensitivity rises (85%→94%), specificity falls (76%→52%)
Both rise together, so the largest $\rho$ is best
Sensitivity falls (94%→85%), specificity rises (52%→76%)
Both stay roughly constant, so $\rho$ does not matter
quiz.e: Larger $\rho$ makes treatment look more beneficial, so more patients are recommended: more recurrers caught, more non-recurrers treated unnecessarily. The trend is overall, not strictly monotone (1.5→2.0 goes 85/76 → 84/77).

quiz.q: How did the GIST OPT compare with the PERSIST-5 RCT on external validation?
o: Similar sensitivity (89% vs 91%), higher specificity (70% vs 63%)
Higher sensitivity (91% vs 89%), lower specificity (63% vs 70%)
Both sensitivity and specificity were lower than PERSIST-5
Identical sensitivity, specificity not reported
quiz.e: On 557 Polish patients the OPT had sensitivity 89% and specificity 70%, vs PERSIST-5's 91% and 63%.

quiz.q: For radiotherapy in extremity sarcoma, the RCT's univariate analysis and the OPT found:
o: RCT: age > 60 only significant predictor; OPT: age cutoff 52
RCT: age > 52 only significant predictor; OPT: age cutoff 60
RCT: tumor grade only significant predictor; OPT: age cutoff 52
Both found age > 60 as the only relevant split
quiz.e: The slides contrast the RCT's age > 60 with the OPT cutoff of 52.

quiz.q: After prognostic matching, why can outcome differences between matched treated and untreated patients still not be attributed to treatment?
o: Unobserved confounders remain in the treated arm, unseen by $g_\theta$
Matching on $\|x_i-x_j\|$ discards the prognostic information in $x$
Bucket counts still differ, so the cohorts remain unbalanced
The OPT is trained before matching and ignores the buckets
quiz.e: Matching balances observed baseline risk, but $g_\theta$ never saw why physicians treated; treated patients still do worse than their baseline estimates. Counts are equal by construction.

quiz.q: Why does R.O.A.D. up-weight treated non-recurrences ($\rho>1$) rather than down-weight them?
o: Treated patients' unobserved prognosis is worse, so $h_{t=1}$ overstates risk
Treated non-recurrences are rare, so up-weighting only fixes class imbalance
Down-weighting would make the MIO matching problem infeasible
Untreated patients have worse unobserved prognosis, so $h_{t=0}$ is too low
quiz.e: Unobserved confounding makes treated outcomes look worse than the drug's true effect. Increasing $\rho$ pulls $h_{t=1}$ toward lower risk to correct that. The class-imbalance reading misses the confounding purpose.

quiz.q: With $\rho=1.5$, predicted 7-year RFS was 79% under imatinib vs 82% without. What follows?
o: Residual confounding still dominates; $\rho$ of at least 2 is needed
Imatinib is harmful here, so the OPT should never recommend it
$\rho=1.5$ is optimal because it maximizes OPT specificity
Matching failed, so buckets must be redefined before tuning
quiz.e: Imatinib is known not to increase recurrence, so the drug looking worse means confounding remains. At $\rho=2$ imatinib RFS (83%) exceeds no imatinib (82%).

quiz.q: A clinician sets $\rho=3.25$ (sensitivity 94%, specificity 52%) instead of $\rho=2$ (84%, 77%). The main cost is:
o: Many more non-recurring patients receive unnecessary imatinib
Many more recurring patients are left untreated
The OPT can no longer be externally validated
The matching step must be re-solved with new buckets
quiz.e: Higher $\rho$ recommends treatment more often: more recurrers caught, but specificity drops from 77% to 52%, so roughly half of non-recurrers get treated.

quiz.q: Why is OPT sensitivity computed on untreated patients who recurred?
o: Their recurrence shows they would have benefited, assuming the drug is effective
Treated recurrers are excluded because they were used to train $g_\theta$
Untreated patients have no confounding, so labels are unbiased
Recurrence is only recorded for untreated patients
quiz.e: An untreated recurrer is a patient who needed treatment, provided imatinib would have prevented the recurrence. That assumption is explicit on the slide.

quiz.q: The sarcoma OPT reached sensitivity 90% but specificity only 15%. The slides interpret this as:
o: The OPT can spare 15% of non-benefiting patients from RT given to everyone today
The OPT fails, since specificity below 50% is worse than random
Most patients should not receive RT after limb-sparing surgery
The OPT is overfit because sensitivity is close to 100%
quiz.e: Current practice gives RT to all limb-sparing surgery patients (specificity 0%), so 15% is a gain while keeping 90% sensitivity.

written.q: Describe how R.O.A.D. turns an observational cohort into one that emulates an RCT. Write the per-bucket matching formulation, explain each constraint, and state what this step does and does not correct.
written.m: Train $g_\theta$ on untreated patients ($t_i=0$) to predict recurrence and apply it to all patients, giving baseline risk $w_i=g_\theta(x_i)$. Split patients into $m$ buckets of baseline risk. In bucket $k$, with treated set $S_1^k$ and untreated set $S_0^k$, solve $\min_z\sum_{i\in S_1^k}\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|$ s.t. $\sum_{j\in S_0^k}z_{ij}=1\ \forall i\in S_1^k$, $\sum_{i\in S_1^k}z_{ij}\le1\ \forall j\in S_0^k$, $z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$. The first constraint matches each treated patient to exactly one control; the second prevents reusing a control; binaries make it an assignment problem. Objective: matched pairs close in covariates. Result: $n_1^k=n_0^k$ per bucket, so within a risk stratum treatment is equally likely, reducing prognostic heterogeneity like an RCT. It does not correct unobserved confounding: $g_\theta$ was trained on $t_i=0$, unobserved factors that drove treatment remain in the treated group, and their outcomes stay worse than their baseline estimates, so matched outcome differences cannot be attributed to treatment.
k: Baseline model trained on untreated, applied to all
Correct MIO objective and both constraints explained
Equal treated/untreated counts per bucket emulate RCT
Unobserved confounding remains; reason tied to $g_\theta$ trained on $t=0$

written.q: Explain the counterfactual models and the Optimal Policy Tree in R.O.A.D. Write the treated-arm loss and the OPT objective, explain the role of $\rho$, and describe how $\rho$ was chosen in the GIST study.
written.m: $h_{t=0}$ is trained on matched untreated patients $S_0$ with loss $\frac1{n_0^s}\sum_{i\in S_0}\ell(y_i,h_{t=0}(x_i))$. $h_{t=1}$ is trained on matched treated patients with $\frac{1}{n_1^s}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_1^-}\ell(y_i,h_{t=1}(x_i))+\rho\sum_{j\in S_1^+}\ell(y_j,h_{t=1}(x_j))\Big)$, where $S_1^+$ are treated non-recurrences. Raising $\rho$ makes the model fit those patients better, lowering predicted risk under treatment and offsetting the unobserved worse prognosis of treated patients. The OPT solves $\min_{\tau(\cdot)}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\big(\mathbb 1\{\tau(x_i)=0\}h_{t=0}(x_i)+\mathbb 1\{\tau(x_i)=1\}h_{t=1}(x_i,\rho)\big)$, assigning each leaf the arm with lower total predicted recurrence. Tuning in GIST: $\rho\in[1.5,3.25]$ with survival RFs; at 1.5 predicted 7-year RFS was 79% with vs 82% without imatinib (confounding still visible); at 2, 83% vs 82%, so $\rho\ge2$. Sensitivity and specificity then guide the choice: higher $\rho$ raises sensitivity (85%→94%) and lowers specificity (76%→52%). Convergent sensitivity/specificity across OPTs indicates robustness.
k: Direction: $\rho$ lowers predicted treated risk to offset confounding
OPT objective as predicted recurrence under assigned arm

written.q: Compare the two R.O.A.D. applications (GIST/imatinib and sarcoma/radiotherapy): data source, validation, results, and what each shows about the advantages over standard RCT analysis.
written.m: GIST: observational training data, 536 MSK patients (1982-2017), confounded because higher-risk patients got imatinib; prognostic matching plus $\rho$-weighted counterfactual models. External validation on 557 Polish registry patients: sensitivity 89%, specificity 70%, vs PERSIST-5 RCT 91% and 63%; OPT found three subgroups that do not benefit and two that do, whereas prior work split on one variable at a time. Sarcoma: training on a 164-patient MSK randomized trial (77 brachytherapy, 87 not), stratified by baseline risk with oversampling of higher-risk strata. Validation on 936 MSK patients who did not receive RT: sensitivity 90%, specificity 15% (various OPTs 88-90%, 15-21%). Since RT is given to all limb-sparing surgery patients, the OPT could spare 15% of patients who would not benefit; it found an age cutoff of 52 vs the RCT's univariate age > 60. Lessons: observational data can yield validated, interpretable multivariable subgroups, and RCT data can be used beyond the ATE.
k: GIST: observational, matching + $\rho$, Polish validation numbers
Sarcoma: RCT training data, 936-patient validation numbers
